Reviewer: 2
We thank the reviewer for his/her constructive comments on our work.
<Major points>
Comments:
1. Although the data show that AcrIIA7 predominantly exists as a tetramer in solution, it is
not definitively demonstrated that it binds to tracrRNA in this specific oligomeric state and
whether the tetramer is indeed the sole biologically active unit.
2. It would substantially strengthen the proposed hijacking mechanism to determine whether
AcrIIA7 functions as a monomer, dimer, or tetramer upon RNA binding. Binding assays with
tracrRNA/sgRNA and Cas9 inhibition assays using monomeric or dimeric AcrIIA7 variants
should be performed to confirm that only the tetramer can serve as the functional entity.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this thought-provoking question.
Because AcrIIA7 consistently appears as a tetramer, we considered the tetramer to be the
functional unit and conducted all mechanistic analyses using this native oligomeric state. To
explore the reviewer’s intriguing suggestion regarding potential functions of alternative
oligomeric states, we attempted to generate monomeric or dimeric variants through structure-
guided point mutations. However, none of the mutants disrupted tetramer formation.
To overcome this limitation, we also designed and tested multiple double and triple mutants,
yet the tetrameric assembly remained intact. Finally, we attempted to interfere with
oligomerization by fusing large tags (Trx or MBP) to either the N- or C-terminus, but for
reasons that remain unclear, these tagged constructs also failed to dissociate the tetramer.
As suggested by the extensive intermolecular interfaces observed in the crystal structure,
AcrIIA7 tetramerization appears to be driven by exceptionally strong and widespread
protein–protein interactions, which likely explains why the tetrameric form is highly resistant
to dissociation. We share the reviewer’s enthusiasm for this question, and although we were
unable to obtain variants with separable oligomeric states, we will continue efforts to
generate such constructs in future studies.
Nevertheless, given the remarkable stability of the tetramer and its consistent presence across
all variants we tested, we infer that the tetrameric assembly is intrinsically linked to the
biological activity of AcrIIA7. Thus, although we cannot experimentally exclude the
possibility of other functional states, our data strongly support the tetramer as the biologically
relevant and mechanistically active unit of AcrIIA7.
3. While a direct interaction between ΔN48AcrIIA7 and tracrRNA has been established in
vitro, the study currently lacks in vivo evidence. The authors need to confirm this interaction
in a cellular context, for instance, by performing RNA Immunoprecipitation (RIP) or CLIP-
seq.
Response: We understand the reviewer’s concern. As suggested, we attempted RNA
immunoprecipitation (RIP) experiments; however, due to the numerous variables and
complexities inherent to the cellular environment, we were unable to obtain sufficiently clear
and reproducible results to include in this revision.
Nevertheless, throughout the revision period, we consistently observed robust binding
between AcrIIA7 and tracrRNA in multiple additional experiments. Moreover, we repeatedly
detected a reduction in gRNA formation mediated by AcrIIA7 in cells (Figure 8), and this
decrease in gRNA levels was directly correlated with reduced Cas9 activity (new
Supplementary Fig. 9). Taken together, these independent and converging lines of evidence
strongly support the validity of our model in which AcrIIA7 binds to and hijacks tracrRNA,
thereby preventing efficient gRNA formation and subsequent Cas9 activation.
4. The evidence for gRNA loading inhibition remains indirect. Order-of-addition cleavage
assays imply a pre-assembly effect, but do not directly monitor RNP formation.
5. Additional experiments using separate crRNA and tracrRNA with Cas9 and target DNA,
varying Acr concentration and addition order, or pull-down assays of Cas9-RNA complexes,
would more directly demonstrate inhibition at the loading step.
Response: We agree with the reviewer’s concern regarding the lack of direct evidence for
gRNA-loading inhibition, and we appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to address this
experimentally. Although our model predicted that hijacking of tracrRNA would prevent
proper gRNA assembly and subsequently block its loading onto Cas9, we sought to obtain
more explicit experimental evidence supporting this mechanism.
To this end, we separately synthesized crRNA and tracrRNA and performed experiments in
which their order of addition with Cas9 and AcrIIA7 was systematically varied. Although
activation of Cas9 using separately prepared crRNA and tracrRNA produced lower activity
than using a pre-assembled sgRNA, Cas9 activity was still detectable (Supplementary Fig. 9).
When tracrRNA or gRNA encountered AcrIIA7 before interacting with Cas9, Cas9 activity
was completely inhibited in all cases. However, when the RNAs first interacted with Cas9 to
form a fully assembled RNP complex, AcrIIA7 was no longer able to inhibit Cas9 activity.
These results clearly demonstrate that AcrIIA7 cannot inhibit Cas9 once the RNP complex
has been formed and that AcrIIA7 exerts its inhibitory effect by binding to tracrRNA or
gRNA prior to RNP assembly. This new evidence is presented in Supplementary Fig. 9 and
incorporated into the main text.
If the reviewer still finds the evidence for gRNA-loading inhibition insufficient despite these
additional experiments, we are willing to focus our interpretation solely on tracrRNA
hijacking and remove the statement that AcrIIA7 blocks gRNA loading onto Cas9 after
hijacking.
6. Physiological relevance of gRNA formation assays: The authors should discuss whether
the faint bands in Figure 7 are physiologically relevant, and clarify if their findings reflect
physiological inhibition potential or an artifact of the RNA-only annealing assay.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the physiological
relevance of the faint gRNA bands. Based on our additional analyses, we would like to
clarify the following points:
(1) Correlation between gRNA formation and AcrIIA7-mediated inhibition (Figure 7 and
Figure 3).
In the presence of AcrIIA7, gRNA formation decreases in a concentration-dependent manner,
and the extent of gRNA assembly varies depending on whether AcrIIA7 encounters crRNA
or tracrRNA first. These trends correlate well with our in vitro order-of-addition inhibition
assays, in which AcrIIA7 effectively inhibits Cas9 only when it binds the RNA components
prior to RNP formation. Thus, the faint gRNA bands observed in Figure 7 reflect biologically
meaningful RNA intermediates whose formation is directly linked to the inhibitory
mechanism.
(2) Physiological relevance demonstrated by additional revision experiments (Supplementary
Fig. 9).
In response to another reviewer2’s comment (comments 4&5), we performed further
experiments using separately synthesized crRNA and tracrRNA instead of sgRNA to more
precisely determine the stage at which AcrIIA7 inhibits Cas9. As expected from the faint
gRNA formation in vitro, Cas9 activity was substantially reduced compared to reactions
using sgRNA. Importantly, however, these faint gRNA were sufficient to activate Cas9, and
AcrIIA7 fully inhibited Cas9 activity whenever it encountered tracrRNA before Cas9.
Conversely, when crRNA and tracrRNA met Cas9 first to form a complete RNP, AcrIIA7
failed to inhibit Cas9.
Taken together, these results demonstrate that although gRNA formation is inefficient under
RNA-only in vitro conditions, the faintly assembled gRNA species are biologically
meaningful, as they directly correlate with Cas9 activity and AcrIIA7-mediated inhibition.
We have incorporated this interpretation into the Discussion section as suggested by the
reviewer.
7. The data suggest that AcrIIA7 recognizes structural features of tracrRNA rather than
sequence. Experiments with compensatory mutations disrupting/restoring stem-loop pairing,
or truncated RNAs containing minimal motifs, would provide direct evidence for structure-
dependence in RNA recognition.
8. Have the authors performed any assays, such as CLIP-seq or in vitro footprinting, to
identify the precise binding sequence between AcrIIA7 and tracrRNA? Determining the exact
binding region would greatly help in understanding the proposed tracrRNA hijacking
mechanism.
Response: We first thank the reviewer for raising this important and previously overlooked
question. If AcrIIA7 binds tracrRNA, identifying which region of tracrRNA mediates this
interaction is indeed a critical issue. While structural analysis of the AcrIIA7–tracrRNA
complex would provide the most definitive insight—and such studies are currently underway
in our laboratory with promising preliminary progress—we agree that defining a minimal
binding motif represents an important and complementary line of investigation.
Guided by this reviewer’s suggestion, we synthesized a series of gRNA variants in which
individual stem–loop elements were selectively removed and examined their interactions with
AcrIIA7 using EMSA. Removal of stem–loop 3 (SL3) did not abolish binding, although the
affinity for AcrIIA7 was noticeably reduced. In contrast, gRNA variants lacking both SL2
and SL3, or lacking all three stem–loops (SL1–SL3), showed little to no detectable binding to
AcrIIA7. These results indicate that SL3 is not strictly required for binding, whereas SL1 and
SL2 are essential. We therefore conclude that SL1 and SL2 constitute the minimal structural
motif necessary for AcrIIA7 recognition.
These new findings identifying the minimal tracrRNA-binding motif have been incorporated
into the Results section as a newly added subsection and are presented in Figures 6C, 6D,
and 6E.
9. Given that the head domain is located near the predicted RNA-binding groove, it is
important to rule out any influence of the affinity tag on RNA binding or Cas9 inhibition. A
comparison with tag-cleaved or N-terminally tagged constructs would be helpful and may be
necessary.
Response: We thank this reviewer for raising this important point. Our AcrIIA7 constructs
were originally expressed with a C-terminal 6x His tag, and we agree that the presence of the
affinity tag could potentially influence RNA binding or Cas9 inhibition. To directly address
this concern, as requested by the reviewer, we generated an additional N-terminally tagged
version of the pdAcrIIA7 N48 construct and compared its RNA-binding with that of the C-
terminally tagged protein. Both constructs exhibited comparable binding affinity toward
sgRNA in our EMSAs, indicating that the presence or position of the affinity tag does not
interfere with the RNA binding mechanism of AcrIIA7. These results support that the
functional conclusions presented in this study are not affected by tag.
This result has been described in the main text and is now presented together with the new
Supplementary Fig. 6.
10. The authors conclude, based on SEC co-elution, that AcrIIA7 does not interact with Cas9.
The authors are encouraged to temper their interpretation accordingly and, if possible, to
perform complementary experiments capable of detecting transient or weak interactions in a
cellular context.
Response: We appreciate for the reviewer’s insightful suggestion. In agreement with this
recommendation, we performed pull-down assays to examine whether AcrIIA7 can interact
with SpyCas9 in a cellular context, which would allow detection of weak or transient
interactions that may not be captured by SEC co-elution analysis. These experiments were
performed using both full length pdAcrIIA7 and the ΔN48 variant. In all cases, we did not
observe detectable interaction between SpyCas9 and either AcrIIA7 construct under the
tested conditions. These results support the conclusion that AcrIIA7 does not directly bind
SpyCas9 as part of its inhibitory mechanism, consistent with our SEC analysis. The results of
this pull-down experiment have been compiled in the new Supplementary Fig. 4 and have
also been incorporated into the main text.
11. In Figure 5, the RNA-only band intensity remains similar across protein concentrations,
while in the tracrRNA assays, the free RNA band is nearly absent in the sgRNA EMSA. (i)
Have lower protein concentrations been tested to resolve shifts more clearly? (ii) Quantifying
band intensities to estimate binding affinities (e.g., Kd values) would strengthen the
conclusions.
Response: As suggested by the reviewer, we attempted to determine the dissociation constant
(Kd) through repeated experiments. However, we found that accurately estimating Kd values
based on band intensities was technically challenging, and the resulting values were not
sufficiently reliable. For this reason, we did not include these data in the current revision.
We are currently conducting structural studies of the AcrIIA7–tracrRNA complex and are
obtaining promising results. In future follow-up studies, we plan to determine the binding
affinity between AcrIIA7 and tracrRNA using more quantitative and definitive approaches,
such as surface plasmon resonance (SPR) or isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). We
sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion.
12. In Figure 5b, the band shift appears to change depending on protein concentration. Could
this be due to conformational changes of AcrIIA7 or tracrRNA, or are there other possible
reasons?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for carefully observing this subtle change, which
we had not previously considered. Based on the reviewer’s comment, we have reflected on
this point, and our interpretation is as follows. When the protein binds to specific RNA, the
RNA may bend or become compacted, altering not only its molecular mass but also its shape
and net charge, which leads to nonlinear changes in electrophoretic mobility. Therefore, as
the protein concentration increases and more protein molecules bind to the more RNA,
numerous RNA species with subtle structural changes are formed, which likely explains the
slight differences observed in the band positions.
<Minor points>
1. In Figures 2E and 2F, the specific residues are not clearly distinguishable. To improve
clarity, the authors should use distinct colors or labeling to unambiguously highlight each
residue being discussed.
Response: We have revised the figure according to the reviewer’s suggestion to make the
residues more clearly visible.
2. In Figures 3D and 3E, additional labeling would help clarify the specific regions being
highlighted and allow readers to better distinguish between domains or datasets.
Response: We have revised the figure according to the reviewer’s suggestion.
3. In Figures 3, 7C, and 7D, the notation for incubation order could be improved. Please
specify explicitly that the numbers shown correspond to the order of incubation.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. We have revised Figures 3, 7C,
and 7D to explicitly indicate the order of incubation. The numbers shown in each panel now
clearly represent the sequential incubation steps, as described in the revised figures.
4. In Figure 4, the SDS-PAGE and SEC profiles of SpyCas9 show heterogeneity and possible
aggregation.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. The SEC and SDS-PAGE profiles of
SpyCas9 indeed showed slight heterogeneity, which is likely due to partial aggregation
commonly observed for Cas9 proteins at high concentrations. We have now included a note
in the revised figure legend to clarify this observation.
5. The legends for Figure 5B and 5G are incomplete. They should explicitly state that the lane
labeled 'B' represents the 'buffer only' control.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We have revised the legends for
Figures 5B, 5F, and 5G to explicitly indicate that the lane labeled “B” represents the sgRNA
in buffer control.
6. In Figure 5G, the two bands observed in the EMSA experiment with full-length pdAcrIIA7
and tracrRNA are insufficiently explained. Clear annotation of these bands is recommended.
Similarly, in Figures 5C, 5D, 5F, and 5G, the identity of specific bands should be clarified by
additional labeling, as was done in Figure 5B.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. We have revised Figures 5C,
5D, 5F, and 5G to clearly annotate the identity of each band, following the labeling format
used in Figure 5B.
The appearance of two bands in Figure 5G is somewhat ambiguous. This phenomenon was

revealed that this head domain is not essential for tracrRNA binding and is highly flexible.
Therefore, it is plausible that the presence of two bands is due to structural heterogeneity
resulting from the flexible head domain, leading to different conformational states of
AcrIIA7. We have included this interpretation in the revised manuscript.
7. The abbreviations used in Figure 6F (DW, Pd, Me) are not defined. Please specify their
meanings in the figure legend for clarity.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this helpful comment. We have revised the legend of
Figure 6F to define all abbreviations (DW, Pd, and Me) for clarity.

9. n Figures 3, 7C, and 7D, the notation for incubation order could be improved. Please
specify explicitly that the numbers shown correspond to the order of incubation.
Response: Following the reviewer’s recommendation, we improved the notation describing
the incubation order in Figures 3, 7C, and 7D. In the revised figures, the numbers explicitly
indicate the sequential order of component addition, where ‘1’ represents the components that

Response: We agree with the reviewer’s point and find it valid. However, in the context of a
typical structure–function study, we believe that both structural analysis and subsequent
investigation of the functional unit are equally important components for elucidating the
mechanism. Therefore, we consider it a reasonable and strategic approach to present these
two aspects as separate sections within the Results, each contributing distinct and essential

Reviewer: 3
We thank the reviewer for his/her constructive comments on our work.
<Major points>
Comments:
1. The mutational studies identify the tracrRNA binding site in the protein, but what motif in
tracrRNA is responsible for the binding is not clarified. the minimal sequence with the major
binding affinity for AcrIIA7 needs to be investigated.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this important question and providing
valuable comments. Reviewer 2 raised a similar point, underscoring the significance of this
issue. Our response is as follows.
If AcrIIA7 binds tracrRNA, identifying which region of tracrRNA mediates this interaction is
indeed a critical issue. While structural analysis of the AcrIIA7–tracrRNA complex would
provide the most definitive insight—and such studies are currently underway in our
laboratory with promising preliminary progress—we agree that defining a minimal binding
motif represents an important and complementary line of investigation.
Guided by this reviewer’s suggestion, we synthesized a series of tracrRNA variants in which
individual stem–loop elements were selectively removed and examined their interactions with
AcrIIA7 using EMSA. Removal of stem–loop 3 (SL3) did not abolish binding, although the
affinity for AcrIIA7 was noticeably reduced. In contrast, tracrRNA variants lacking both SL2
and SL3, or lacking all three stem–loops (SL1–SL3), showed little to no detectable binding to
AcrIIA7. These results indicate that SL3 is not strictly required for binding, whereas SL1 and
SL2 are essential. We therefore conclude that SL1 and SL2 constitute the minimal structural
motif necessary for AcrIIA7 recognition.
These new findings identifying the minimal tracrRNA-binding motif have been incorporated
into the Results section as a newly added subsection and are presented in Figures 6C, 6D,
and 6E.
2. The authors claim AcrIIA7 shows tracrRNA-specific binding, but the RNA-binding
experiments were conducted only for crRNA and tracrRNA. Since AcrIIA7 work in bacterial
cells including numerous cellular RNA species, the authors need to address whether AcrIIA7
specifically binds tracrRNA than other cellular RNAs. A reliable method may be a pull-down
assay using AcrIIA7 as a bait followed by sequencing of bound RNAs.
Response: We understand the reviewer’s concern. As suggested, we attempted pull-down
assay using AcrIIA7 as a bait; however, due to the numerous variables and complexities
inherent to the cellular environment, we were unable to obtain sufficiently clear and
reproducible results to include in this revision.
Nevertheless, throughout the revision period, we consistently observed robust binding
between AcrIIA7 and tracrRNA in multiple additional experiments. Moreover, we repeatedly
detected a reduction in gRNA formation mediated by AcrIIA7 in cells (Figure 8), and this
decrease in gRNA levels was directly correlated with reduced Cas9 activity (new
Supplementary Fig. 9).
In addition, through several experiments performed during the revision period—including
binding assays with type II-C tracrRNA (Figure 6A), binding assays using ssRNA engineered
to adopt the same structure as tracrRNA (Figure 6B), and experiments aimed at identifying
the minimal binding motif (Figures 6C, 6D, and 6E)—we demonstrated that AcrIIA7 binds
tracrRNA in a structure-specific manner. These results suggest that AcrIIA7 discriminates
tracrRNA from other cellular RNAs based on its unique structural features. We have
incorporated these findings into both the Results and Discussion sections of the manuscript.
<Minor points>
1. In the proposed functionl mechanism, as far as I understand, AcrIIA7 should be a viral
protein, not a bacterial protein. Does AcrIIA7 from Phocaeicola dorei mean that the gene is
identified from sequencing from total bacterial DNA, infected by virus and thus including
viral DNA? If so, this needs to be clearly explaind.
Response: Yes, that is correct. This gene originates from a bacteriophage and was transferred
into the bacterial chromosome through phage infection. As the reviewer suggested, we have
clarified the origin of this gene in the Introduction section, where we explicitly describe this
point as follows;
“The pdAcrIIA7 gene originates from a bacteriophage, but as is the case for many Acr genes,
it is incorporated into the bacterial chromosome through phage infection”
2. The indicaton of the full name of pdAcrIIA7 is missing.
Response: We indicated the meaning of pdAcrIIA7 in introduction.
3. AcrIIA7 seems to strongly bind both free tracrRNA or gRNA? Would the protein be able
to dissociate crRNR and tracrRNA? If so, this could be added in the inhibitory mechanism.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this highly intriguing topic. Whether AcrIIA7 is
capable of dissociating pre-assembled crRNA-tracrRNA duplexes is indeed an important
mechanistic consideration. Based on our current data, however, AcrIIA7 does not appear to
disrupt the crRNA-tracrRNA complex once it is formed. In our gRNA formation assays,
pdAcrIIA7 did not reduce the gRNA band when added after crRNA-tracrRNA duplex
formation (Fig. 8C), indicating that it does not dissociate the pre-assembled gRNA. In
contrast, meAcrIIA7, which has an affinity for gRNA, produced band shifts even in the
presence of gRNA, but this likely reflects its binding to the stem-loop region of tracrRNA
within the gRNA structure, not dissociation of the duplex itself (Fig. 8D). Furthermore, our
mapping experiments show that AcrIIA7 binds to the stem-loop region of tracrRNA, which is
distinct from the repeat-anti repeat base pairing interface between crRNA and tracrRNA.
Because the AcrIIA7 binding site does not overlap with the crRNA-tracrRNA region, it is
unlikely that AcrIIA7 actively separates the two RNAs. Instead, AcrIIA7 appears to bind the
structured region of tracrRNA or gRNA without disrupting the crRNA-tracrRNA pairing.
Together, these results suggest that AcrIIA7 inhibits Cas9 not by dissociating crRNA and
tracrRNA, but rather by binding to the stem-loop region of tracrRNA and preventing proper
gRNA formation and loading onto Cas9.
We have incorporated this important discussion into the “Discussion section” of the
manuscript.
4. In Fig 5G, tracrRNA shows a single band, which is completely shifted by 2.5 uM
pdAcrIIA7. But in Fig 7A, tracrRNA is in two bands, which is not much shifted at the same
protein concentration. This conflict needs to be addressed.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s careful observation. The difference in tracrRNA
band patterns between Figures 5G and 7A arises from the distinct buffer conditions used in
each experiment. In Figure 5G, tracrRNA was incubated with pdAcrIIA7 in a buffer
containing 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0) and 75 mM NaCl, which produces a single, well-
defined RNA band that is fully shifted at 2.5μM pdAcrIIA7.
In contrast, the assay in Figure 7A essentially required inclusion of the RNA annealing buffer
for crRNA–tracrRNA duplex formation, resulting in a different final composition (10 mM
Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA). This altered ionic strength and the presence of
EDTA affect the folding state and electrophoretic mobility of tracrRNA, producing two
bands, and also influence the binding affinity and shift behavior of pdAcrIIA7.
To avoid misinterpretation, each gel includes buffer-matched controls, ensuring that
comparisons are made only within identical experimental conditions. Therefore, although
Figures 5G and 7A show different migration patterns and shift efficiencies, these differences
reflect buffer-dependent RNA behavior, not inconsistencies in AcrIIA7 function.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The CRISPR–Cas9 system provides adaptive immunity against invading genetic elements through a
dual-RNA-guided DNA cleavage mechanism. This system relies on the precise assembly of a
ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex composed of the Cas9 endonuclease, a CRISPR-derived RNA
(crRNA), and a trans-activating CRISPR RNA (tracrRNA). Around 100 anti-CRISPR proteins that
inhibit CRISPR–Cas systems have been identified, and the mechanisms by which they act are
increasingly being elucidated. However, the inhibitory mechanisms of many Acrs, including AcrIIA7,
remain poorly understood. Here, we present the structure of AcrIIA7 and uncover a previously
unrecognized mechanism by which it inhibits Cas9 function. Structural and biochemical analyses reveal
that AcrIIA7 specifically binds to tracrRNA, preventing its association with crRNA and thereby
blocking formation of the active Cas9 RNP complex. This tracrRNA hijacking mechanism represents a
unique strategy for CRISPR inhibition, in which an anti-CRISPR protein targets an RNA scaffold
essential for Cas9 activation rather than interacting directly with the Cas9 protein. Our findings provide
the first structural insight into tracrRNA-targeted anti-CRISPR activity and highlight RNA–RNA
interaction interfaces as vulnerable nodes in CRISPR–Cas immunity.

---

## Introduction

CRISPR–Cas systems provide adaptive immunity in bacteria and archaea by recognizing and destroying
invading genetic elements such as bacteriophages and plasmids 1-4. CRISPR-Cas systems are
categorized into two main classes, Class1 and Class2, based on their locus composition and effector
protein organization, and further divided into six types (I-VI)5,6. Class 1 CRISPR–Cas systems, which
include types I, III, and IV, are composed of multi-subunit RNA-guided surveillance complexes, while
Class2 CRISPR-Cas systems, exemplified by type II systems, utilize a single effector protein, such as
Cas9 7-9. Among these, the Type II-A CRISPR–Cas9 system from Streptococcus pyogenes (SpyCas9)
has been most extensively characterized and widely repurposed for genome engineering 10,11. The Cas9
endonuclease is guided to its DNA target by a dual-RNA complex composed of a CRISPR-derived
RNA (crRNA) and a trans-activating CRISPR RNA (tracrRNA), which together form a stable RNA
duplex that enables specific recognition and cleavage of target DNA 10,12. The assembly of this
ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex is a critical step in the activation of Cas9 function8,13-15.

To counteract CRISPR-mediated immunity, bacteriophages and mobile genetic elements have evolved
anti-CRISPR (Acr) proteins that inhibit various stages of the CRISPR–Cas immune pathway 16-19. Since
the initial discovery of Acr proteins in 2013 18, approximately 100 distinct variants have been identified
through a combination of functional screening and bioinformatic analyses 20-22. Due to the frequent lack
of sequence homology and shared structural features among Acrs, their classification is primarily based
on the specific CRISPR–Cas systems they inhibit 18,23,24.

These proteins employ diverse mechanisms to disrupt CRISPR-Cas activity, including inhibition of
DNA binding, interference with nuclease activity, or sequestration of essential cofactors 17,22,25-28. Most
recently, AcrIF25 was reported to inhibit CRISPR function by binding to Cas7 and preventing the
formation of a DNA-cleaving complex 28. Among these, AcrIIA proteins are known to inhibit Cas9, yet
for many members of this family, the molecular mechanisms of inhibition remain poorly defined.
AcrIIA7 is one such anti-CRISPR protein that has been previously shown to inhibit SpyCas9, but its
mechanism of action remained elusive 29. Recent study also showed that AcrIIA7 might be a phage-
encoded anti-CBASS protein that inhibits host cyclic-oligonucleotide-based immunity by sequestering
cyclic dinucleotide (CDN) molecules 30. Our current study was designed to elucidate the molecular
mechanism underlying the inhibition of Cas9 by AcrIIA7. In this study, we determined the high-
resolution crystal structure of AcrIIA7 from Phocaeicola dorei (hereafter called pdAcrIIA7) and
conducted structure-based functional analyses to elucidate its inhibitory mechanism. The pdAcrIIA7
gene originates from a bacteriophage, but as is the case for many Acr genes, it is incorporated into the
bacterial chromosome through phage infection. Strikingly, we found that AcrIIA7 does not interact with
Cas9 directly, but instead binds to tracrRNA with high specificity and affinity. This interaction prevents
tracrRNA from forming a duplex with crRNA, thereby blocking the formation of the functional Cas9
RNP complex and ultimately inhibiting Cas9 activity. This mechanism represents a previously
uncharacterized mode of anti-CRISPR action that we refer to as tracrRNA hijacking.

Our findings provide the first structural and mechanistic insight into how an anti-CRISPR protein
targets the RNA component of the CRISPR–Cas9 system rather than the Cas protein itself. This
discovery not only expands our understanding of anti-CRISPR diversity but also highlights RNA–RNA
interactions as a underexplored axis of vulnerability in CRISPR-mediated immunity. The tracrRNA
hijacking strategy employed by AcrIIA7 may represent a broader class of anti-CRISPR mechanisms and
opens avenues for the design of synthetic CRISPR inhibitors that operate via RNA targeting.

---

## Results

The structural studies revealed that AcrIIA7 from Phocaeicola dorei is composed of three
domains, and among them, the head domain is flexible

The investigation into the inhibition mechanism of AcrIIA7 commenced with the overexpression and
purification of the full-length pdAcrIIA7, paving the way for subsequent structural analysis. The
purification process involved Ni-NTA affinity chromatography followed by size exclusion
chromatography (SEC), where distinct peak was observed. SDS-PAGE analysis confirmed the purity of
the pdAcrIIA7 protein in the main peak eluted around 14mL (Fig. 1A). Crystallizations trials using
protein samples eluted from the main peak were successful, and diffraction data from a single crystal
were collected at the PAL synchrotron. Initial molecular replacement (MR) phasing, using a predicted
structural model from Alphafold2, was unsuccessful. To resolve the phasing issue, we performed
SelenoMet labelling for the purpose of Se-SAD phasing, which ultimately determined the 2.16 Å
structure of pdAcrIIA7. The final structural model was refined to R = 20.12 % and R = 25.14 %.
work free
The diffraction data and refinement statistics are summarized in Supplementary Table 1.

The crystal belonged to space group P2 2 2 and contained four molecules (Molecule A ~D) in the
1 1 1
asymmetric unit (ASU) (Fig. 1B). The final structural model showed that molecules B and C of
pdAcrIIA7 covered most of pdAcrIIA7 (residues M1 to E150), while molecules A and D excluded 22
and 28 N-terminal amino acids, respectively, due to unclear electron density. The structure of
pdAcrIIA7 consisted of seven α-helices (α1–α7) and seven 𝛽–sheets (𝛽1–𝛽7) (Fig. 1C and D).
Following the two long helices of head domain (α1 and α2), the core domain is formed by five 𝛽-
sheets(𝛽1,𝛽2 and 𝛽5-𝛽7) and three α-helices (α3,α4 an d α7), extending further two α-helices (α5–α6)
and two 𝛽-sheets (𝛽3–𝛽4) as extended domain (Fig. 1C and D). Four molecules in the same ASU
exhibited slight structural differences in their head domains (α1–α2) and in the α7 regions of their core
domains (Fig. 1E~G). RMSD analysis indicated that molecules B and A differed by 1.8Å, whereas
molecules B and C, as well as molecules B and D, showed relatively larger disparities with RMSD
values of 2.6Å and 2.2Å, respectively (Fig. 1E). Furthermore, the α1 and α2 helices in the head domain
of molecules B and C were found to be inclined at different angels (Fig. 1F). In the core domain, the
alpha helix was well conserved in molecules A and B, while in molecules C and D, these regions
formed a loop configuration rather than alpha helix (Fig. 1G).

An analysis of the electrostatic potential on the molecular surface revealed a distinct distribution of
charges; negative charges were predominantly localized in the head and the extended domains, whereas
positive charges were primarily concentrated in the core domain (Fig. 1H). B-factor analysis highlighted
notable rigidity in the core and head domains, evidenced by their low B-factor values (average 48.12Å).
In contrast, the extended domain exhibited high B-factor values (average 68.98Å), indicating greater
structural flexibility (Fig. 1I).

The utilization of the DALI server to explore proteins structurally akin to pdAcrIIA7 revealed the
sulfate transporter protein as the most structurally similar (Fig. 1J). Despite the sulfate transporter
emerging as the closest match, the modest Z-score (6.0) and sequence identity (5%) underscored a
discernible lack of structural congruence. In addition, the other selected proteins exhibited similarly low
Z-scores (ranging from around 5.7-4.6) and sequence identities (2~10%), collectively signifying the
novelty of the AcrIIA7 structure. Indeed, the fold of pdAcrIIA7 appears to be unprecedented within the
existing structural repertoire. While we were preparing our manuscript, the structure of Tad2 (AcrIIA7
from human gut metagenomic libraries) was published, which represented a form of AcrIIA7 lacking
the head domain and anti-CRISPR activity 30.

Since the MR phasing method using the predicted structural model by Alphafold2, failed, we were
intrigued to compare the predicted model with the experimental structure. To achieve this, we aligned
two structures. The structural alignment of pdAcrIIA7 with the Alphafold2 predicted model revealed
notable differences. Although the overall fold was the consistent between the two models, significant
structural discrepancies were observed in the head domain. The α1 and α2 helices in the predicted
model were notably distorted, and several regions did not match when compared to the crystal structure
of pdAcrIIA7 (Fig. 1K). These structural discrepancies could explain the unsuccessful MR phasing.
Overall, based on the structural studies of pdAcrIIA7, we concluded that pdAcrIIA7 is composed of
three domains, and among them, the head domain is flexible.

AcrIIA7 forms a distinct and robust homo-tetrameric structure in solution
Indeed, although numerous Acrs inhibit Cas9 activity as monomers, previous research has
demonstrated that some Acrs operate in a dimeric configuration 31,32. In the case of pdAcrIIA7, the SEC
results indicated that pdAcrIIA7 eluted between the molecular sizes of 158kDa and 44kDa, producing a
prominent peak in the chromatogram (Fig. 1A). However, SEC alone was insufficient to determine the
stoichiometry of pdAcrIIA7. To confirm its stoichiometry, we employed multi-angle light scattering
(MALS) analysis. MALS yielded an experimental molecular weight of 74.86 kDa, with a fitting error of
1.12 % (Fig. 2A). Given the theoretically calculated molecular weight of monomeric pdAcrIIA7 with a
C-terminal 6X histidine tag is 17.82 kDa, the MALS data conclusively indicated that pdAcrIIA7 exists
as a tetramer in solution. This tetrameric structure of pdAcrIIA7 provides further insights into the
diverse mechanisms of Acr function, revealing that higher-order oligomerization may play a crucial role
in their ability to inhibit Cas9 activity.

Further crystallographic packing analysis revealed three types of putative dimers: Mol B(D)/Mol A(C),
Mol B(A)/Mol C(D), Mol B(A)/Mol D(C) (Fig. 2B and C). To ascertain the biologically relevant form,
we conducted protein-protein interface (PPI) analysis using the PDBePISA server 33. The PPI analysis
showed complexation significance score (CSS) for each dimer: Mol B(D)/Mol A(C) (0.000), Mol
B(A)/Mol C(D) (0.100), and Mol B(A)/Mol D(C) (1.000). Notably, the Mol B(A)/Mol D(C) dimer
exhibited the greatest biological relevance, as indicated by its superior CSS compared to other dimers
with lower scores (Fig. 2B).

Upon closer examination of each dimer’s structural details, it was observed that the Mol B/Mol A dimer
formed through a loop connecting 𝛽5 to α7 in the core domain, forming 2 hydrogen bonds between
G133 and Q138 of each molecule. (Fig. 2D) The Mol B(A)/Mol C(D) dimer predominantly interacted
through 5 hydrogen bonds in the core domain, with an additional hydrogen bond in the head domain
(Fig. 2E). In the case of Mol B/ Mol D dimer, which scored the highest in CSS, displayed a more
intricate interaction pattern with 14 hydrogen bonds and 6 salt bridges between two molecules,
primarily in both the core domain and the extended domain (Fig. 2F).

Anti-CRISPR activity of AcrIIA7 relies on the absence of its head domain
To evaluate the inhibitory effect of AcrIIA7 on the enzymatic activity of Cas9, we established an in
vitro target DNA cleavage assay. We selected Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 (SpyCas9) for this assay
due to its known anti-CRISPR activity against SpyCas9 and its widespread use in genome-editing
applications. SpyCas9 is a large nuclease composed of 1368 amino acid residues. The assay employed
an 1100bp double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) substrate containing the target region with the PAM
sequence (5’-NGG-3’), along with a specifically designed single guide RNA (sgRNA) to direct
SpyCas9 to the target site. We tested varying concentrations of AcrIIA7 to quantitatively assess its
inhibitory potential. As expected, when SpyCas9 was incubated with sgRNA to form the
ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex, the enzyme successfully cleaved the target DNA (Fig. 3A). The
inhibitory capacity of AcrIIA7 was further evaluated by varying the incubation order of the components.
Despite using a final AcrIIA7 concentration of 10 μM, which is much higher than the effective
concentrations of other AcrIIA family members, AcrIIA7 did not inhibit DNA cleavage of SpyCas9
under any tested condition (Fig. 3A). Given that previous studies have identified AcrIIA7 from human
gut metagenome (meAcrIIA7) as an inhibitor of SpyCas9, we decided to align the sequences of
pdAcrIIA7 and meAcrIIA7 to identify potential differences. Sequence alignment revealed that
pdAcrIIA7 possesses an additional 48 residues at the N-terminus (Fig. 3B). Apart from this notable
difference, the sequences were largely conserved between the two proteins (Fig. 3B). Structurally, these
extra 48 residues found in pdAcrIIA7 correspond to the head domain (Fig. 3C and D). Leveraging the
experimental structure of the complete AcrIIA7, we constructed a model depicting the tetrameric
arrangement of the meAcrIIA7 (Fig. 3E). To ascertain the functionality of pdAcrIIA7 in the absence of
the head domain, we engineered a head domain-deleted pdAcrIIA7 (ΔN48AcrIIA7)), subsequently
conducting a comparative analysis with the intact pdAcrIIA7, ΔN48AcrIIA7, and the meAcrIIA7.

The stoichiometries of ΔN48AcrIIA7 and meAcrIIA7 were analyzed through MALS. The results
revealed an experimental molecular weight of 52.46 kDa for the ΔN48 AcrIIA7 and 52.79 kDa for the
meAcrIIA7. Considering the theoretically calculated molecular weight of both monomeric
ΔN48AcrIIA7 and meAcrIIA7 to be around 12.7 kDa, the MALS data demonstrated that the
ΔN48AcrIIA7 and the meAcrIIA7 exist as a tetramer in solution. This observation indicated that the
absence of the head domain does not impede tetrameric formation (Fig. 3F and G).

In the in vitro cleavage-inhibition assay using SpyCas9, both the meAcrIIA7 and the ΔN48AcrIIA7
were subjected in the same experimental conditions as the full-length pdAcrIIA7. In contrast to the full
length pdAcrIIA7, which did not exhibit inhibitory function in this assay, the meAcrIIA7 and
ΔN48AcrIIA7 variants displayed significant inhibition of DNA cleavage. Notably, a distinct non-
cleaved band was observed, particularly when the ANcrIIA7 was pre-incubated with sgRNA (Fig. 3H and
I). Further assays examining concentration and order dependency with ΔN48AcrIIA7 demonstrated that
inhibition increased with higher concentrations , but only when AcrIIA7 was added prior to Cas9 RNP
complex formation (Fig. 3J). These findings suggest that the head domain of pdAcrIIA7 interferes with
its inhibitory functions, rendering the full length pdAcrIIA7 unable to impede DNA cleavage.
Additionally, DNA recovery was observed only when AcrIIA7 was introduced before the assembly of
the SpyCas9-sgRNA complex, indicating that AcrIIA7 likely inhibits Cas9 activity by preventing proper
RNP formation and thereby obstructing target DNA recognition.

AcrIIA7 inhibits the DNA cleavage activity of Cas9 without directly binding to the protein
Acr proteins are known to employ diverse strategies to inhibit Cas9, with many acting directly on the
Cas9 protein to suppress its DNA cleavage activity 31,34-36. Previous studies have demonstrated that
numerous Acrs achieve inhibition by physically blocking key functional domains of Cas9, such as the
HNH or RuvC nuclease domains 35, REC3 domain34, BH domain37, and WED-PI domain 38. Building
upon these findings, we further investigated the inhibition mechanism of AcrIIA7 through binding
assays conducted with full-length Cas9 proteins from multiple species, including Streptococcus
pyogenes (SpyCas9), Neisseria meningitidis (NmeCas9), Haemophilus parainfluenzae (HpaCas9), and
Simonsiella muelleri (SmuCas9). These experiments were designed to identify potential cross-species
interactions and to determine whether AcrIIA7 exhibits a conserved inhibitory mechanism across
different Cas9 variants. When purified AcrIIA7 was mixed with various Cas9 proteins, no co-migrations
were detected with any of the Cas9 variants upon the SEC experiments, suggesting that AcrIIA7 does
not directly bind to Cas9 to exert its inhibitory activity (Fig. 4A and Supplementary Fig. 1A~C). Given
that the full-length AcrIIA7 was confirmed to be inactive, we conducted the identical binding assay
using meAcrIIA7 and the ΔN48AcrIIA7 to determine if the presence of the head domain hindered
interactions between AcrIIA7 and Cas9. The assay also showed no binding results, indicating that,
regardless of the presence of the head domain, AcrIIA7 inhibits DNA cleavage independently of
directly binding to Cas9 (Fig. 4B and C, and Supplementary Fig. 2A~C and 3A~C). We also performed
pull-down assays to examine whether AcrIIA7 can interact with SpyCas9 in a cellular context, which
would allow detection of weak or transient interactions that may not be captured by SEC co-elution
analysis. Pull-down experiments were performed using both full length pdAcrIIA7 and the ΔN48
variant. In all cases, we did not observe detectable interaction between SpyCas9 and either AcrIIA7
construct under the tested conditions (Supplementary Fig. 4). These results support the conclusion that
AcrIIA7 does not directly bind SpyCas9 as part of its inhibitory mechanism, consistent with our SEC
analysis.

Due to the potential ambiguity of analyzing co-migration tendency of AcrIIA7 with full length Cas9s
using SEC based experiments, we additionally performed binding assays with distinct functional
domains of SpyCas9, including RuvC, REC, HNH, WED, and PI. Each domain was expressed and
purified (REC1-2, REC3, HNH and WED), except for the PI domain, which was insoluble in our
experiments (Supplementary Fig. 5A). We conducted the SEC binding tests between each domain of
SpyCas9 and both full length pdAcrIIA7 and ΔN48AcrIIA7. These experiments demonstrated that
neither full-length pdAcrIIA7 nor ΔN48AcrIIA7 exhibited obvious co-migration with various domains
of Cas9, suggesting that the inhibitory mechanism of AcrIIA7 operates independently of direct binding
to Cas9 (Supplementary Fig. 5B~I).

AcrIIA7 lacking head domain directly binds RNA, specifically tracrRNA
Despite the inhibitory activity of AcrIIA7 has been validated through in vitro assays, its precise
mechanism of action remains elusive due to limitations of previous binding assays with Cas9 proteins.
To gain further insight into its functional properties, we analyzed the surface electrostatic potential of
tetrameric pdAcrIIA7, as the electrostatic characteristics of a protein surface are often closely linked to
its biological function. This analysis revealed that a deep groove is formed toward the core domain of
the AcrIIA7 tetramer, and that this groove is lined with numerous positively charged residues (Fig. 5A).
Based on this observation, we hypothesized that the protein may be capable of binding to nucleotides.
To explore whether AcrIIA7 directly binds to nucleotides, we initially performed EMSA using sgRNA
that has been used for the formation of active SpyCas9. The result showed a clear RNA band super-shift
when RNA was incubated with both ΔN48AcrIIA7 and meAcrIIA7, but no shifts were observed with
full-length pdAcrIIA7, indicating that only AcrIIA7 without the head domain directly binds to sgRNA
(Fig. 5B). This finding aligns with previous experimental results of in vitro assay, which also revealed
that only AcrIIA7 without the head domain inhibited DNA cleavage, demonstrating that the head
domain-deleted AcrIIA7 directly binds to sgRNA to inhibit the Cas9-mediated DNA cleavage.
Interestingly, in the case of sgRNA, an upper shift of the band was observed even in the absence of
protein, when only buffer was added (Fig. 5B). This shift was presumed to result from structural
changes in the sgRNA under the buffer conditions. However, the protein-induced super-shift appeared
at a distinctly higher position, allowing clear differentiation between nonspecific buffer effects and
specific binding of the protein (Fig. 5B). Because the C-terminal His-tag of AcrIIA7 could potentially
affect its interaction with RNA, we generated an N-terminally tagged version of AcrIIA7 and examined
its binding to sgRNA. The N-terminally tagged protein exhibited the same binding behavior
(Supplementary Fig. 6), indicating that the presence and position of the tag does not influence RNA
interaction.

We next asked whether AcrIIA7 also binds to other types of nucleic acids. EMSAs with ssDNA and
dsDNA showed no band shifts in the presence of AcrIIA7, indicating its specific interaction with RNA,
but not DNA (Fig. 5C and D).

The guide RNA (gRNA) in bacteria and generated sgRNA used for our assay consists of two
components: CRISPR-derived RNA (crRNA), which specifically binds to target DNA with its
complementary sequence, and trans-activating CRISPR RNA (tracrRNA), which binds to Cas9 to form
Cas9-RNP complex (Fig. 5E). To comprehensively understand the binding mode of AcrIIA7 to gRNA,
we performed additional EMSA with crRNA and tracrRNA, respectively. AcrIIA7 did not exhibit band
shifts with crRNA (Fig. 5F), while super-shifts were detected with tracrRNA (Fig. 5G). Interestingly,
although active AcrIIA7, without head domain; ΔN48AcrIIA7 and meAcrIIA7 showed super-shifts with
tracrRNA, full-length pdAcrIIA7 also showed distinct band shifts with tracrRNA (Fig. 5G). These
results suggest that the head domain of pdAcrIIA7 does not significantly affect binding to shorter RNA
molecules like tracrRNA but may impose steric hindrance when interacting with longer RNAs such as
sgRNA. One additional noteworthy observation is that pdAcrIIA7 constructs containing the head
domain show two distinct bands in the EMSA with tracrRNA (Fig. 5G). The presence of two bands
might be due to structural heterogeneity resulting from the flexible head domain, leading to different
conformational states of AcrIIA7.

AcrIIA7 binds nucleic acids in a structure-dependent fashion
After confirming that AcrIIA7 binds tracrRNA, we wondered whether this interaction is RNA-specific,
sequence-specific, or instead driven by recognition of a particular stem–loop structure within the
tracrRNA. To address this question, we synthesized the tracrRNA from an Haemophilus parainfluenzae
(Hpa) strain belonging to the type II-C system, which contains a completely different stem–loop
architecture (Fig. 6A), and examined its binding to AcrIIA7 using EMSA. The results showed that
neither pdAcrIIA7 nor the head domain–deficient AcrIIA7 bound to the type II-C tracrRNA with the
distinct stem–loop structure (Fig. 6A). This finding indicates that AcrIIA7 recognizes and interacts with
RNA in a structure-dependent manner, binding only to tracrRNAs that possess a specific structural
configuration. These results indicate that AcrIIA7, which has been reported to inhibit type II-A systems,
indeed acts in a type II-A–specific manner, and that this specificity arises from recognition of a
particular tracrRNA structural feature rather than from RNA sequence alone.

We next asked whether AcrIIA7 binds specifically to RNA, and what would happen if a DNA molecule
possessed a stem–loop structure similar to that of tracrRNA. To address this question, we synthesized an
ssDNA containing the same stem–loop architecture as the type II-A tracrRNA (Supplementary Fig 7).
We refer to this molecule as structured ssDNA (SssDNA) and examined its interaction with AcrIIA7 by
EMSA. Interestingly, both meAcrIIA7 and Δ48AcrIIA7, which lack the head domain, were able to bind
SssDNA, whereas pdAcrIIA7 did not show detectable binding (Supplementary Fig 7). Although the
presence of the head domain in pdAcrIIA7 may slightly interfere with DNA binding, the observation
that AcrIIA7 variants bind to a stem–loop–containing DNA clearly demonstrates that AcrIIA7 does not
interact with nucleic acids in an RNA-specific or sequence-specific manner. Rather, AcrIIA7 recognizes
and binds nucleotides in a structure-dependent fashion.

If AcrIIA7 binds nucleotides containing three stem–loop structures, an important next question is which
stem loops (SL) are specifically recognized and what constitutes the minimal binding motif within
tracrRNA. To address this question, we synthesized a series of gRNA variants (SL12, SL1, SL0) in
which individual stem–loop elements were selectively removed (Fig. 6B) and examined their
interactions with AcrIIA7 using EMSA (Fig. 6C and D). Removal of SL3 did not abolish binding,
although the affinity for AcrIIA7 was noticeably reduced (Fig, 6C and D). In contrast, gRNA variants
lacking both SL2 and SL3, or lacking all three stem–loops (SL1–SL3), showed little to no detectable
binding to AcrIIA7 (Fig. 6C and D). These results indicate that SL3 is not strictly required for binding,
whereas SL1 and SL2 are essential. We therefore conclude that SL1 and SL2 constitute the minimal
structural motif necessary for AcrIIA7 recognition.

tracrRNA binds within the deep groove formed by the AcrIIA7 tetramer core, which is lined with
positively charged residues
To investigate how AcrIIA7 recognizes and binds to tracrRNA, we first identified functionally
important and evolutionarily conserved residues within AcrIIA7 using the Consurf server 39. This
analysis revealed that conserved residues are primarily located in the core domain, with a few also
present in the head domain, including E6 and E10 (Fig. 7A~C). Among these, we focused on conserved
positively charged residues positioned within the deep groove formed by the core domains upon
tetramerization, as they may play a critical role in RNA binding (Fig. 7D). Based on this reasoning, we
selected five conserved, positively charged residues—K58, K66, K71, K93, and R101—as candidates
likely involved in RNA interaction. Supporting this hypothesis, an AlphaFold3 model of the AcrIIA7–
tracrRNA complex showed that tracrRNA fits into the deep groove of the core domain, forming
interactions with these positively charged residues, further reinforcing our prediction (Fig. 7E).

To experimentally validate these predictions, we introduced charge- or size-disrupting mutations by
substituting each residue with aspartic acid or tryptophan, generating five mutants: K58D, K66W,
K71W, K93W, and R101W. Since the N-terminally truncated form (ΔN48) of AcrIIA7 shows the most
distinct RNA binding behavior (Fig. 5B and G), all mutations were introduced into the ΔN48
background. We then examined the RNA-binding ability of these mutants using EMSA with sgRNA.
As expected, the K58D, K66W, and K71W mutants failed to form any detectable complex with sgRNA,
showing complete loss of RNA binding (Fig. 7F). In contrast, K93W and R101W showed an upper-
shifted band indicative of complex formation, but the shifts differed from that of the wild-type,
suggesting altered or weakened binding (Fig. 7F).

To further corroborate these findings, an in vitro cleavage-inhibition assay was performed using the
mutant variants. The results were consistent with those of the sgRNA binding assays: the K58D and
K71W mutants displayed significantly reduced Cas9 inhibitory activity due to their diminished affinity
for sgRNA (Fig. 7G). For the K93W and R101 W mutants, which showed slightly weaker band shifts in
the sgRNA EMSA, a corresponding reduction in cleavage-inhibition activity was also observed
compared to the wild type (Fig. 7G).

Although the K66W mutant, previously shown to have completely lost sgRNA-binding affinity,
exhibited instability at 37℃, preventing target DNA detection in the in vitro assay, results from other
mutants collectively confirmed that sgRNA binding by pdAcrIIA7 is essential for its Cas9 cleavage-
inhibition mechanism. These findings underscore the critical role of conserved, surface-exposed
positively charged residues within the deep groove of AcrIIA7 tetramer in mediating tracrRNA
interactions and inhibiting Cas9 activity (Fig. 7F and G).

The proposed scenario of AcrIIA7-mediated Cas9 inhibition
Based on our series of experimental results, we propose a previously uncharacterized inhibitory
mechanism for AcrIIA7, in which it hijacks tracrRNA to prevent gRNA formation, thereby inhibiting
Cas9 activity. This mode of inhibition represents a previously uncharacterized strategy among known
anti-CRISPR proteins. To validate that tracrRNA hijacking by AcrIIA7 directly impairs gRNA
formation, we synthesized crRNA_repeat and anti-repeat_tracrRNA, and incubated them in annealing
buffer at 37℃ for 2 hours to mimic gRNA formation. The gRNA, formed via annealing of the
complementary repeat and anti-repeat regions, was visualized as an upper band on native gel. Despite
testing multiple annealing conditions, optimal gRNA formation remained challenging. Nevertheless, a
distinct band corresponding to gRNA was detected, allowing us to assess AcrIIA7-mediated inhibition
under these conditions (Supplementary Fig. 8A~C).

Both full length pdAcrIIA7 and meAcrIIA7 were tested for their ability to inhibit gRNA formation.
As protein concentrations increased, the intensity of the gRNA decreased, indicating that AcrIIA7 inhibits
gRNA assembly in a concentration-dependent manner through tracrRNA sequestration (Fig. 8A and B,
Supplementary Fig. 9A and B). Notably, pdAcrIIA7 inhibited gRNA formation completely at 20μM,
whereas meAcrIIA7 achieved the same effect at just 2μM, demonstrating a tenfold greater potency. This
supports the idea that while the head domain of pdAcrIIA7 does not eliminate its ability to bind
tracrRNA, it reduces binding efficiency, particularly in the Phocaeicola dorei-derived AcrIIA7 variant.

Order of addition experiments further confirmed the role of AcrIIA7 in gRNA formation. For full length
pdAcrIIA7, when crRNA and tracrRNA were pre-incubated before AcrIIA7 addition, gRNA formation
proceeded effectively (Fig. 8C and D, Supplementary Fig. 9C and D). However, when AcrIIA7 was
added prior to or simultaneously with both RNAs, gRNA formation was significantly impaired (Fig. 8C
and Supplementary Fig. 9C). In contrast, meAcrIIA7 exhibited potent inhibition regardless of the
incubation order, consistent with its higher affinity for tracrRNA (Fig. 8D and Supplementary Fig. 9D).
These findings collectively demonstrate that AcrIIA7 directly disrupts gRNA formation through
tracrRNA hijacking, thereby blocking CRISPR-Cas activity.

Although our model predicted that hijacking of tracrRNA would prevent proper gRNA assembly and
subsequently block its loading onto Cas9, we sought to obtain more explicit experimental evidence
supporting this mechanism. To this end, we separately synthesized crRNA and tracrRNA and performed
experiments in which their order of addition with Cas9 and AcrIIA7 was systematically varied.
Although activation of Cas9 using separately prepared crRNA and tracrRNA produced lower activity
than using a pre-assembled sgRNA, Cas9 activity was still detectable (Supplementary Fig.10). When
tracrRNA or gRNA encountered AcrIIA7 before interacting with Cas9, Cas9 activity was completely
inhibited in all cases. However, when the RNAs first interacted with Cas9 to form a fully assembled
RNP complex, AcrIIA7 was no longer able to inhibit Cas9 activity (Supplementary Fig. 10). These
results clearly demonstrate that AcrIIA7 cannot inhibit Cas9 once the RNP complex has been formed
and that AcrIIA7 exerts its inhibitory effect by binding to tracrRNA or gRNA prior to RNP assembly.

In conclusion, inhibitory strategy of AcrIIA7 centers on tracrRNA hijacking, which serves as the
foundation for its two inhibitory effects: (1) halting gRNA maturation through tracrRNA sequestration
and (2) preventing the assembly of the Cas9-RNP complex by blocking gRNA loading onto Cas9 (Fig.
9).

## Methods

Cloning, overexpression, and purification of AcrIIA7s, various Cas9 from different species, and
various Cas9 domains for structural and biochemical studies
The gene encoding AcrIIA7 (residues 1–150) from Phocaeicola dorei (accession number:
WP_038611802) was synthesized by Bionics (Daejeon, Republic of Korea) and subsequently inserted
into a pET21a plasmid vector (Novagen, Madison, WI, USA), equipped with a C-terminal hexa-
histidine tag for affinity chromatography. Cloning was executed utilizing NdeI and XhoI restriction
sites. Following transformation into Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) competent cells, a single colony was
selected and cultured in lysogeny broth (LB) medium for protein expression. For preparation of
selenomethionine-labeled protein used in crystallographic studies, cells were alternatively grown in 1L
SelenoMet Medium base supplemented with 50mL SelenoMet Nutrient mix and 4 mL SelenoMet
solution (Molecular Dimension). For generation of the N-terminally histidine-tagged AcrIIA7, the
AcrIIA7 coding sequence was additionally cloned into the pET28a vector using the same NdeI and XhoI
restriction sites, with a stop codon introduced at the C-terminus to prevent C-terminal tagging.
Following transformation into E. coli BL21(DE3) competent cells, protein expression was carried out in
LB medium. For all expression cultures, cells were grown at 37°C with 50 μg/mL ampicillin or 25
μg/mL kanamycin, until the optical density at 600 nm reached 0.7–0.8, upon which 0.25 mM isopropyl-
β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) was added. The subsequent incubation, at 20°C for 18 hours in a
shaking incubator, facilitated protein expression.

Following culture harvest via centrifugation at 2350 × g and 20°C for 15 minutes, the cells were
resuspended in 20 mL lysis buffer (20 mM Tris–HCl pH 8.0 and 500 mM NaCl) and lysed via
ultrasonication at 4°C. The resulting lysate and supernatant were separated by centrifugation at 27,000 ×
g and 4°C for 30 minutes. The supernatants were collected, combined with Ni-nitrilotriacetic acid
(NTA) affinity resins, and incubated at 4°C for 2 hours. Subsequently, the mixture was loaded onto a
gravity-flow column, and after elution, the resin-bound AcrIIA7 was eluted using elution buffer (20 mM
Tris–HCl pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, and 250 mM imidazole).

Further purification of target protein samples was performed by size exclusion chromatography (SEC)
on a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column connected to an ÄKTA Explorer system. Eluted
fractions were pooled, concentrated to 10 mg/mL, and subjected to structural and biochemical analyses.
Protein sample purity was assessed by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis
(SDS-PAGE).

Additionally, expression constructs for Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 (#62731), Neisseria meningitides
Cas9 (#71474), Haemophilus parainfluenzae Cas9 (#121540), and Simonsiella muelleri Cas9 (#121541)
were procured from Addgene. The SpyREC12, SpyREC3, SpyHNH, and SpyWED domain expression
constructs were generated via cloning assays utilizing S. pyogenes Cas9 plasmids as templates. All PCR
products were subsequently cloned into the pET28a vector using NdeI and XhoI restriction sites. The
Cas9 proteins and domains were cultured in lysogeny broth (sigma-lennox), expressed, and purified
using the same methodology as for AcrIIA7.

Oligonucleotide sequences and plasmid information are provided in Supplementary Data 1. Plasmids
generated in this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

Crystallization and X-ray diffraction data collection
Crystallization of pdAcrIIA7 was executed in a controlled environment at 20°C employing the sitting
drop vapor diffusion technique. Initial crystals were achieved by combining 1 μL of protein solution
(10.23 mg/mL protein in SEC buffer) with 1 μL of reservoir solution (comprising 20%(w/v) PEG 3000
and 0.1M acetate pH 4.5) and equilibrating the mixture using 0.5 mL of reservoir solution. The
definitive crystals utilized for X-ray diffraction analysis were cultivated on plates, with a solution
comprising 1 μL of protein solution and 1 μL of reservoir solution containing 15% (w/v) PEG 3000 and
0.1M acetate pH 4.7 over three days.

Following crystal growth, a single crystal was carefully chosen and immersed in a reservoir solution
augmented with 23% (v/v) glycerol for cryoprotection. X-ray diffraction data acquisition was conducted
at -178°C utilizing the BL-5C beamline at the Pohang Accelerator Laboratory (Pohang, Korea).
Subsequent data processing, encompassing indexing, integration, and scaling, was performed using
HKL2000 software 42.

Structure determination and refinement.
The initial structure of pdAcrIIA7 was determined using AutoSol, SAD phasing, an automated
experimental phasing with model building software, in the package of PHENIX 43. Subsequent model
building with refinement was performed using phenix.autobuild, phenix.refine, and Coot 44,45. The
structure quality and stereochemistry were validated using the MolProbity46. All structural figures were
generated using the PyMOL program 47. Representative electron density map was provided at
Supplementary Fig. 15

Multi-angle light scattering analysis (MALS)
SEC-coupled multi-angle light scattering (SEC-MALS) experiments were carried out to determine the
absolute molecular mass of AcrIIA7 in solution. Purified AcrIIA7 protein in SEC buffer was injected
into a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column pre-equilibrated with SEC buffer. SEC-MALS was
performed at 20 °C with a 0.5 mL/min buffer flow rate. The ÄKTA explorer system (GE Healthcare)
was coupled with a DAWN-Treos MALS detector (Wyatt Technology, Santa Barbara, USA). A
reference molecular mass value was established using bovine serum albumin for calibration. Data were
processed and assessed using ASTRA software (Wyatt Technology).

In vitro anti-CRISPR activity assay
To assess the inhibitory potential of AcrIIA7 and its mutants on Cas9-mediated target cleavage, a series
of in vitro target DNA cleavage assays were conducted. SpyCas9 enzyme, acquired from NEB, a single
guide RNA (sgRNA), generated using the EnGen® sgRNA Synthesis Kit, S. pyogenes (NEB), and each
AcrIIA7 wild-type and its mutant variants were added and combined in different order. For the first
binding, the mixture was incubated at 25°C for an hour. In the subsequent components were added to
the mixture, then incubated at 25°C for 30 minutes. Finally, the target DNA was added to the reactions
and incubated in NEBuffer r3.1(NEB) at 37°C for 25minutes. Proteinase K was added and incubated for
10 minutes to terminate the reaction.

All reaction products were subjected to loading and separation through electrophoresis on 4%
polyacrylamide gels. The visualization of DNA cleavage products was accomplished by staining the
gels with SYBR GOLD. The resulting gel images were analyzed to evaluate the inhibitory impact of the
wild-type AcrIIA7 and the various mutant forms on Cas9-mediated target cleavage.

Size exclusion chromatography assay for complex formation
Size exclusion chromatography (SEC) was employed to investigate whether AcrIIA7 forming
complexes between various Cas9s from different species, or SpyCas9 domains. Each wild-type and N-
term deleted AcrIIA7 from Phocaeicola dorei and AcrIIA7 from metagenome were mixed with various
Cas9s and each Cas9 domain, followed by incubation at 4 °C for 1 hour. Then, the resulting mixture
was loaded onto a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare) pre-equilibrated with
SEC buffer (20 mM Tris–HCl pH 8.0, 150 mM NaCl). The eluted fractions corresponding to the peaks
of interest were collected, and the samples were subsequently analyzed by SDS-PAGE stained with
Coomassie Brilliant Blue. To assess the complex formation between AcrIIA7 and the Cas9 proteins or
each domain, the migration patterns, and the co-migration of protein bands within the gel were
examined and analyzed.

Pull down assay
6x His-tagged SpyCas9 cloned into the pET21a vector and untagged AcrIIA7 cloned into the pET24a
vector were co-transformed into E. coli BL21(DE3) competent cells. A single co-transformed colony
was selected and cultured under the same conditions used for AcrIIA7 expression. Cells were harvested
by centrifugation and resuspended in lysis buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0,150 mM NaCl.
The cell suspension was lysed by sonication, and the clarified lysate was incubated with Ni-NTA
agarose beads for 2 hours to capture 6x His-tagged SpyCas9. After incubation, the bead-protein
complexes were loaded onto a gravity flow column, washed with buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCl pH
8.0,150mM NaCl, 80 mM Imidazole. Bound proteins were eluted with buffer containing 20 mM Tris-
HCl pH 8.0,150 mM NaCl, 250 mM Imidazole. Eluted samples were analyzed by SDS-PAGE and
visualized by Coomassie Brilliant Blue staining.

Mutagenesis
Site-directed mutagenesis was performed utilizing a QuickChange kit obtained from Stratagene (San
Diego, CA, USA), following the manufacturer's instructions. Primer sequences used for mutagenesis are
listed in Supplementary Data 1. The resulting mutations were subjected to sequencing analysis to verify
the precision of the introduced alterations. This step ensured the fidelity of the modifications. Following
successful validation, all mutant protein variants were produced and purified by applying the identical
methodology previously described for the wild-type protein 48.

Electrophoretic mobility shift assay with polyacrylamide gel (EMSA-P)
Each purified target DNA (20 nM), sgRNAs (1 50 nM), crRNA (150 nM), type II-A tracrRNA (150
nM), type II-C tracrRNA (150 nM), structured single strand (Sss) RNA (20 nM), tracrRNA variants
(150 nM) were incubated with AcrIIA7 proteins at room temperature (25°C) for 1 hour. The samples
were then separated by gel electrophoresis at 100 V on a 10 % native 0.5 × TBE (Tris-Borate EDTA)
polyacrylamide gel. After electrophoresis, gels were stained with SYBR Gold (Invitrogen, Waltham,
MA, USA) and visualized according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

For the gRNA formation, synthesized crRNA_repeat (300 nM), and anti-repeat_tracrRNA(300 nM)
were incubated in a buffer containing 10 mM Tris pH 8.0, 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA at 37°C for 2
hours. The formed gRNA complexes were also analyzed by electrophoresis on a 10 % native
polyacrylamide gel in 0.5X TBE buffer and visualized using SYBR Gold dye.

In vitro anti-CRISPR activity assay using separately synthesized tracrRNA and crRNA
To further investigate the order-dependent inhibitory activity of AcrIIA7, additional in vitro target DNA
cleavage assays were performed using crRNA and tracrRNA supplied as separate components. crRNA,
tracrRNA, SpyCas9, and AcrIIA7 were combined in various orders, as specified for each experimental
condition. Depending on the reaction sequence, RNA–AcrIIA7 binding reactions were incubated at 25
°C for 1 hour, whereas crRNA–tracrRNA annealing reactions were incubated for 2 hours in buffer
containing 30 mM Tris–HCl (pH 7.5) and 100 mM potassium acetate. Where indicated, Cas9 was
subsequently added and incubated at 25 °C for 30 minutes. For all conditions, target DNA was added as
the final step in the presence of NEBuffer r3.1 (NEB), followed by incubation at 37 °C for 40 minutes.
Reactions were terminated by the addition of Proteinase K and incubation for 10 minutes.

All reaction products were subjected to loading and separation through electrophoresis on 4%
polyacrylamide gels. The visualization of DNA cleavage products was accomplished by staining the
gels with SYBR GOLD. The resulting gel images were analyzed to evaluate the inhibitory impact of the
wild-type AcrIIA7 and the various mutant forms on Cas9-mediated target cleavage.

Native Polyacrylamide Gel Electrophoresis (Native-PAGE) assay
The binding of AcrIIA7 to cyclic nucleotides was analyzed using Native-PAGE assay. The cyclic
nucleotides used in this study were cGG(c-di-2’-dGMP) and 1’’-2’-gcADPR(2’-cADPR). These cyclic
nucleotides (5, 10, 20, and 50μM) were incubated with 20μM AcrIIA7 at 18°C for 30min. The reaction
mixtures were then loaded onto 5% native polyacrylamide gels and electrophoresed at 120V. After
electrophoresis, the gels were visualized by Coomassie Brilliant Blue staining.
